title: Stationary waves in strings, air columns and microwaves
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can explain stationary-wave formation, identify nodes and antinodes, and determine wavelength from their spacing.
new_learning: Produce and recognise stationary waves on strings, in air columns and with microwaves.
Select suitable adjustments and observations for each apparatus.

evidence_basis.note: Canonical P1 lesson assignment is deferred; none was inferred.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

blocks.title: How can an invisible wave leave a row of fixed clues?
content: A microwave detector slides along a bench and its reading rises, falls almost to zero, then rises again. Nothing in the apparatus is moving along the bench. What is making the repeating pattern?
The same fixed pattern can appear on a string and inside an air column. Today we use what can be adjusted and what can be observed to reveal it.

figure.purpose: Create a concrete puzzle from repeated microwave detector maxima and minima.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper bench sketch with transmitter, metal reflector and a detector shown at several positions with alternating high and low meter readings. Do not label nodes or antinodes.
figure.alt_text: A microwave detector gives alternating high and low readings between a transmitter and reflector.

blocks.title: One experimental recipe, three physical systems
content: In the ideal model, each demonstration needs two waves of the same type, frequency and equal amplitude travelling in opposite directions. Usually one wave is the reflection of the other. Their superposition makes fixed nodes and antinodes. In a real apparatus, losses can make the amplitudes slightly unequal, so measured minima may be small rather than exactly zero.

A node is a point or position on a stationary wave with zero amplitude. An antinode is a position in a stationary wave where the oscillation amplitude is maximum. The apparatus does not show the travelling component waves separately. It shows their fixed resultant pattern.

controlled_definitions.displayed_content: a point or position on a stationary wave with zero amplitude
a position in a stationary wave where the oscillation amplitude is maximum

figure.purpose: Connect incident plus reflected waves to one fixed amplitude pattern.
figure.brief: Three-stage hand sketch: outgoing wave, reflected wave, then resultant envelope with fixed N and A positions. Use sparse coloured arrows and labels.
figure.alt_text: Opposite travelling waves superpose to form fixed nodes and antinodes.

blocks.title: Stretched string: tune until the loops settle
content: A vibrator drives a string that passes over a pulley to a hanging mass. The pulley end reflects the wave. Change the generator frequency, change the vibrating length, or change the tension by changing the hanging mass. At certain settings the string shows steady loops.

Look for fixed positions with almost zero motion and positions between them with maximum motion. A blurred string alone is not enough. The decisive observation is that the amplitude changes from zero or minimum at fixed positions to maximum at other fixed positions.

figure.purpose: Teach the controllable variables and observable signature in the string apparatus.
figure.brief: White-paper apparatus sketch with signal generator, vibrator, string, pulley and hanging masses. Add three adjustment callouts: frequency, length and mass/tension; show stable loops with fixed nodes.
figure.alt_text: A driven string over a pulley forms stable loops when frequency, length or tension is adjusted.

blocks.title: Air column: listen or measure for resonance
content: Place a loudspeaker at the open end of an air column and use a reflecting boundary at the other end. Vary the frequency or the effective air-column length until a large response is detected. A microphone can be moved along the tube to locate repeated minima and maxima.

The air particles form the stationary pattern. A microphone usually responds to pressure variation, so its maxima and minima do not automatically carry the same labels as displacement maxima and minima. Use the stated measured quantity before naming a node or antinode.

figure.purpose: Distinguish the production and observation steps for an air-column stationary wave.
figure.brief: Side-view tube with loudspeaker, movable microphone and reflecting end. Show a frequency-control arrow and a detector-reading strip with alternating maxima and minima. Avoid end-correction language.
figure.alt_text: A loudspeaker and reflecting end produce a stationary wave detected by a movable microphone in a tube.

blocks.title: Microwaves: map the pattern point by point
content: Aim a microwave transmitter at a metal reflector. The incident and reflected microwaves overlap. Slide a detector along the line between them and record positions of repeated signal maxima and minima.

The detector turns an invisible field pattern into a position-reading graph. Adjacent minima, or adjacent maxima, are separated by half a wavelength. This is the same spacing rule used for nodes or antinodes on a string.

figure.purpose: Show how a movable detector maps an invisible stationary microwave pattern.
figure.brief: Plan view with transmitter, metal plate, incident and reflected arrows, detector rail and a small signal-against-position trace. Mark adjacent minima distance d without giving lambda.
figure.alt_text: A detector moved between a microwave transmitter and reflector maps repeated signal maxima and minima.

blocks.title: Two formulas to remember
content: In the spacing formula, d and wavelength lambda are measured in metres. In v = f lambda, wave speed v is in metres per second and frequency f is in hertz.

Suppose adjacent microwave minima are 2.40 cm apart. Then lambda = 2d = 4.80 cm = 0.0480 m. If f = 10.0 GHz, v = (10.0 x 10^9)(0.0480) = 4.80 x 10^8 m s^-1. The arithmetic is correct, but the result is not close to the expected microwave speed, so the measurements or stated frequency should be checked. A physical check can catch a neat but unreliable calculation.

figure.purpose: Model spacing, unit conversion and an independent physical plausibility check.
figure.brief: Annotated working layout with d=2.40 cm, lambda=2d, conversion to metres and v=f lambda. End with a warning symbol beside the implausible speed, not a corrected answer.
figure.alt_text: A microwave spacing calculation is checked against the expected physical scale of wave speed.

blocks.title: Adjust, observe, interpret
content: For a string, adjust frequency, length or tension and observe steady loops with fixed zero and maximum amplitude positions. For an air column, adjust frequency or length and detect a resonant pattern with a microphone or response meter. For microwaves, use a reflector and move a detector through repeated maxima and minima.

A common mistake is to say that a large response alone proves a stationary wave. It feels reasonable because resonance can be loud or dramatic. It fails because one large reading gives no spatial pattern. Evidence is stronger when fixed minima and maxima repeat with position.

figure.purpose: Compare the control, reflection and observation method across all three required experiments.
figure.brief: Three-column hand-drawn comparison table headed string, air column and microwaves, with rows for source, reflector, adjustment and observation. Keep wording short and do not include end corrections.
figure.alt_text: A comparison of how stationary waves are produced and observed in strings, air columns and microwaves.

concepts_taught: experimental production of stationary waves on strings, in air columns and with microwaves
fixed spatial maxima and minima as evidence
misconceptions_addressed: One large response by itself proves a stationary wave.
Every detector maximum is automatically a displacement antinode regardless of the measured quantity.
